author: @akraminabdullah
comment:
So I've been using this phone for 3 months now, and yeah I totally love it. I was an iPhone user, which the last phone I used is the 15 Pro Max. Everything is great to me, but there's a few aesterisks though. Selfie and 0.7x ultra wide is ok, and I don't use those much. Compared to the main and 5x periscope, those camera has insane quality. Rear display really make me love taking selfies with the back camera. I still think that videos are better on iPhones, but this phone's video quality is just as good. Super steady shot, for example, is really steady on straight movements, but struggles a bit at orbit pan shots. Perfomance is great, I never had overheating thanks to it's large vapour chamber. Games however, iPhones are more optimized for that, for example especially supercell games — my iPhone 11 Pro also runs 60hz like my 15 PM and Xiaomi. Haptics are objective in my opinion — they're much stronger with the Xiaomi, but I hope that there are more haptic patterns like what we take for granted in iPhones. Speakers are loud. Display is very smooth and rarely stutters. I'm using the Chinese ver btw. Yes, it's a little difficult to use it, but I just get used to it and have minimal problems personally

Will I recommend the Xiaomi? It's not that easy of a recommendation, but I totally am happy having this one over the iPhone. There are also very few people that uses the Xiaomi at my region, and everyone are just impressed of the Xiaomi. If you're reading this far, thank you — I very rarely make comments

author: @carlospro1204
comment:
The iPhone Air—way more profitable for Apple than the Pro. Think about it: it’s close enough to a Pro to carry a similar price tag, but with much less hardware overall—one camera instead of three, a smaller battery, one speaker, and no vapor chamber. If Apple wants to increase revenue with less hardware innovation, this is a perfect way to do it. It’s flashy enough to entice users into purchasing it, leaving the company with higher margins.

Now, don’t you find it interesting that the iPhone Pro has more radical, less conventional, less familiar color options and a new form factor? Could it be that Apple is trying to push buyers toward the more profitable iPhone Air?

comment: Galaxy XR definitely has great value for the price. Vision Pro doesn't have many XR/VR apps, but like the Galaxy XR, it does have its App Store apps that are available on iPad. Unfortunately & Fortunately, Apple lets developers opt out of having their apps on the Vision Pro. I'm sure the Galaxy XR will still lack in content that same way Vision Pro did, but it might gain content quicker thanks to its price and OS. Also naturally, Galaxy XR has a YouTube app because the OS is Android XR, from Google. One thing I'd like to see compared is polish. Apple is quite known for quality & polish in its UI & design. I'm also not a fan of the permanent decision of having the bulky back part of the Galaxy XR, even if it balances out the weight. I wish they found a way to make modular like the Vision Pro. I can imagine this will get annoying when trying to lay back to watch a movie especially since the biggest use-cases for these premium headsets are for watching shows & movies.

author: @Sweet-Vermouth
comment:
For those wondering how this works, this is an oversimplified version - 
Each pixel has 3 photo-diodes each sensitive to different colors of light (RGB). When you open your camera, a voltage is applied across every diode. In the dark very little current is allowed to pass through the diode. The more light falls on the photo-diode, the more current it allows to pass through it. If a very bright light falls on the diode, a lot of current passes through the diode causing it to burn out and permanently allow current to pass through. 
If the camera is not on, there is no voltage across the diode so no current will flow through it when bright light shines on it. The sensor will not be affected if the camera is not on.

If you work hard enough, you should never really have a “zero-click” problem. But there is an extraordinary amount of weirdness happening online nowadays.

comment:
I’m glad I came across this video.
I am a bookkeeper with a technical mind but I am also an educator.
Whilst I love writing technical content, I find marketing these days more and more confusing (albeit fascinating)
The pressure of using AI is also massive (and you really have to wonder why)
So I started to explore it, but for me the one thing it wasn’t really doing was saving that much time when creating content.
When I write a blog article for my website, as I normally write more “technical” content I don’t need AI to give me content ideas.
I still do my research (as I still need to learn the ins and outs of what I am writing to then service my clients)
I still structure the article 
When it comes to writing is when I get AI to help me.
- sometimes I write the content and asks AI to review it and give suggestions on how to make it “better”. I still never copy AI suggestions, I always “mesh” AI suggested content with my own.
Other times I have an idea on how to present the content but I ask AI to draft it for me (I always ask for multiple options)
I then take the various option drafts and put together by adding my own. Then get AI to review my output and once the final piece of content is always a mesh between my work and AI assistance.
I thought it was because I was old school and couldn’t let go of the control.
This video seems to have confirmed that this approach is actually the right one!
